tathābhūta (page 240) eva jātaḥ iti na asya darpaṇarūpatā sattvam | nanu rūpam--------------- kathaṃ miśrībhavet sapratighadharmatvāt tasya | atra āha nahi iti | tatra taddarśanamiti hi yadi niṣpratighatvaṃ, tadālokarūpe'pi tadantargataghaṭādisahasre samasti; ekatāpattistu na hastidarpaṇarūpayorapi atra ghaṭarūpayoriveti samānam | nanu ādarśa eva ayamitthaṃbhūta ityasti pratipattiḥ | atra āha bhrāntirevahi iti | eṣeti ghaṭasya darpaṇātmatā bhramajñānopakalpitā, natu tattvam | nanu evaṃ nīlasya kathaṃ prakāśamānatā jñānasyaiva prakāśadharmatvādityāśaṅkāṃ vyapohati jñānasya caivam iti | na khalu nīlaṃ prakāśate, jñānamevatu ātmanā prakāśamānamanātmanā api prakāśate iti nīlaprakāśarūpa- jñānaprakāśa eva nīlaprakāśa ityetadāyātamaṅgīkāryameva | kuta āyātam | āha arthādarthāvabhāsanasya anihnavanīlamayatvāt jñānalakṣaṇasya ca arthasya anādisiddhaivaṃbhūtasvabhāvatvāt | nanu ātmānātmanorvirodhāt kathaṃ tadubhayaprakāśamanekasya rūpaṃ bhavet, arthaśca aṇusthūlātmā ṣaṭkayogaraktāraktādidoṣaduṣṭa iti | atra āha atraiva iti ubhayarūpatvasamarthane saṃvedanasya avasāyagrahaṇena idamāha-vastuto'tra bādho'sambhavatvādeva parihṛto vastunaḥ saṃkucitātmano deśataḥ kālataśca aṇurūpasya kṣaṇikasya virodhābhāvāt jñānasya ca anādisiddhatayā svabhāvatvāt, kevalaṃ tathā niścetumaśaktāḥ paraiḥ śuṣkatarkakarkaśairasannyāyairjīyante iti | asya iti jñānasvabhāvasya pratibhāsamānasya ca bāhyasya abādhitasaṃvedanasākṣikasya ullaṅghane svacchandavāditvamāpadyeteti vitānanārthinā bāhyārthasiddhigrantho'tra smartavyaḥ | etat neti yaduktaṃ, tatra hetumāha yataḥ iti | anena ca dṛṣṭāntasamarthanena svacchasya vilakṣaṇarūpāntarāvabhāsasāmarthyena vyāptiruktā | tathaiva iti darpaṇāntarāvasthānena | (page 241) bhavataiva iti pratītisiddhaṃ na apahnavanīyamiti vadateti ayamāśayaḥ | tataḥ iti evamabhidhānāt | deśāntarastha iti yaḥ satyasaṃmato hastī, sa eva tāvadasau na tato deśabhedena avabhāsāt, tata eva sa pratisaṃkrānta iti nistattvaṃ bhāṣāmātramadaḥ, nāpi hastyantaravat
**The will as cause, agent, and action** The whole vimarśa has argued that causality is the conscious knower's agency. Now comes the sharpest objection of all, and it threatens to undo everything. If consciousness is *one* — if all the world is a single consciousness and the difference of things is only ignorance — then how is action possible at all? For action needs an agent and an object, two distinct things; but if all is one, there is no distinct object for the agent to act upon. Abhinavagupta's answer is that action is the one *will-to-do* that joins the agent and the object. The jar and the consciousness are, by appearance, two. But there is a single re-recollection (parāmarśa) marked by the will-to-do — the moment "I will make this" — which rests, as it were, in the other consciousness-essence and binds the two together. It is this one will-recollection, and not any external contact, that makes the jar an object of action and consciousness its agent. Without it there is no action, even in a perfectly unified consciousness. But here Abhinavagupta turns on the very idea that the difference is a mere "ignorance." If consciousness is one, and the difference is ignorance, then we must ask: *of whom* is this ignorance? The one-form Brahman cannot have an ignorance that is the mere absence of something else. Nor can the separate souls exist — they too would be raised up by the ignorance. If the ignorance is called "un-explainable" (anirvācya), then we still do not know whose it is; "it shines and yet is un-explainable" is the speech of a yakṣa, a being we cannot pin down. And in fact the difference is real: our cognition rests in difference as it does not rest in non-difference, and the very "refutation" that would remove difference is itself a manifestation — and so would be difference, and so would be ignorance. The whole attempt to dismiss the world as an un-explainable illusion cuts the horns of the hare's head and plucks the sky-flower. Even if we appeal to the revealed teaching, that teaching too would be ignorance — a net of illusions. (And indeed, as Abhinavagupta will say, "even Brahman with ignorance is [admitted by some], so this is not an absolute monism either.") What, then, of the division of the powers — will in the Lord, knowledge in Sadāśiva, action in Īśvara? This is not a separation of real things; it is one action-power, seen under different aspects. The action-power in the action is nothing other than the will. As the teaching says, "the three subtle powers dwell in harmony." And the grammarians' own analysis confirms it: the action-tattva is seen in the agent even when the other adjuncts are absent, and is not seen when the agent's complement is absent — so by presence-and-absence, it is the *resting in the agent* alone that is the action. Even where no explicit agent appears — "here it does not cook" — the agents fit for cooking and enjoying are manifest, implied by the locus. Action is not a thing that happens to an inert object; it is the will at rest in the knower. And so the final synthesis: the will (icchā) itself is the cause-ness, the agent-ness, and the action. The three are one act of consciousness. The cause does not cause, the agent does not act, the action does not move — all three are the one will, by which the Lord, wishing to stand, becomes the world of jar and cloth and all the appearances. This is the action-power: the will of the one consciousness, which is at once what causes, what acts, and what is done. With this, the fourth vimarśa of the kriyādhikāra — the reflexive-awareness of the cause-effect relation — comes to its close. ---

> The sharpest objection to the unity: if consciousness is one and the difference of things is mere > ignorance, how is action possible? For action needs an agent and an object, distinct; but if all is > one, there is no distinct object. Abhinavagupta first answers with the will-to-do — the single > re-recollection marked by the will that joins the agent and the object. > > Then he challenges the premise that the difference is ignorance. If the difference were an > "un-explainable" ignorance, of whom would it be? The one-form reality cannot have an ignorance that > presupposes a duality to be absent from; the separate souls cannot bear it, since they are supposed > to be produced by it; and "un-explainable" is a refusal to answer, not an answer. The difference is > real: cognition rests in difference as it does not rest in non-difference. > > The passage establishes that the difference cannot be an un-explainable ignorance. The full positive > account of the difference (as the self's own manifestation) is developed elsewhere.
